1: # Production MCP connection fix plan
2: 
3: Status: proposed  
4: Prepared: 2026-09-17  
5: Target client: OpenCode (using LM Studio/Qwen as its model provider)
6: 
7: ## Outcome
8: 
9: Make `https://mcal.hajnal.space/mcp` a standards-compatible, authenticated
10: Streamable HTTP MCP endpoint that OpenCode can authorize with OAuth and use to
11: call CommonCal tools.
12: 
13: OpenCode is already the MCP client. LM Studio supplies the model and Qwen is the
14: model; neither replaces the MCP client. No additional MCP client is required.
15: MCP Inspector may be used only as an independent diagnostic tool.
16: 
17: ## Verified current state
18: 
19: Production was probed on 2026-09-17:
20: 
21: - `POST /mcp` with `initialize` reaches the service but returns JSON-RPC
22:   `-32601 Method not found`.
23: - unauthenticated `tools/list` returns nine names, without complete MCP tool
24:   schemas.
25: - unauthenticated `tools/call` returns `401`, but its `WWW-Authenticate` header
26:   points to `http://127.0.0.1:3001/...` rather than the public production URL.
27: - protected-resource metadata at
28:   `https://mcal.hajnal.space/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` is valid JSON
29:   and advertises `https://cal.hajnal.space` as the authorization server.
30: - `https://cal.hajnal.space/.well-known/openid-configuration` returns the
31:   CommonCal SPA HTML, not authorization-server metadata.
32: - `opencode mcp auth commoncal-production` fails on `initialize` before OAuth
33:   discovery can begin.
34: 
35: This means production is reachable but is not currently connectable by a
36: standard MCP client.
37: 
38: ## Confirmed root causes
39: 
40: ### 1. Production does not implement the MCP lifecycle
41: 
42: The production route mounts a custom Axum handler
43: (`mcp-server/src/main.rs:54-78`). Its dispatcher recognizes only `tools/list`
44: and `tools/call`; every other method, including `initialize`, returns `-32601`
45: (`mcp-server/src/gateway.rs:103-185`). Authentication is performed only inside
46: the `tools/call` branch (`mcp-server/src/gateway.rs:214-254`), so OpenCode never
47: receives an OAuth challenge for its initial request.
48: 
49: The custom wire responses are also incomplete:
50: 
51: - `tools/list` emits only `{ "name": ... }`, with no description or
52:   `inputSchema`, and does not preserve the JSON-RPC request id
53:   (`mcp-server/src/gateway.rs:187-212`).
54: - tool results use project-specific serialization rather than SDK-generated MCP
55:   content/result envelopes.
56: 
57: `rmcp` is already a production dependency, and the repository contains a
58: working SDK-backed reference in `slice1-lab/src/bin/mcp_echo.rs`. That lab
59: supports initialization, Streamable HTTP sessions, typed schemas, OAuth
60: middleware, and all tool categories. It explicitly says it is not the
61: production server (`slice1-lab/src/bin/mcp_echo.rs:1-13`).
62: 
63: ### 2. The production OAuth challenge and JWT contract are inconsistent
64: 
65: Both production 401 builders hard-code the lab protected-resource URL
66: (`mcp-server/src/gateway.rs:456-541`).
67: 
68: The JWT validator says it uses discovery, but actually fetches
69: `<issuer>/.well-known/oauth-jwks` directly
70: (`mcp-server/src/oauth.rs:304-350`). It must instead fetch authorization-server
71: metadata and follow its `jwks_uri`.
72: 
73: Production also requires private namespaced claims such as
74: `https://commoncal.tld/user_id` and a custom scope array
75: (`mcp-server/src/oauth.rs:24-46,158-177`). The proven authorization server and
76: lab validator use standard claims: numeric `sub`, `client_id`, space-delimited
77: `scope`, `jti`, and `amr` (`slice1-lab/src/jwt.rs:12-33,147-184`). A token from
78: the repository's own authorization server would therefore still be rejected by
79: the production MCP server.
80: 
81: ### 3. The authorization service is not deployed or routed in production
82: 
83: The production Flux kustomization includes only core and MCP
84: (`deploy/flux/overlays/production/kustomization.yaml:3-5`). The existing auth
85: HelmRelease is excluded and was deliberately removed because PostgreSQL was not
86: available (`deploy/PROBLEM-02-remove-auth.md`). Consequently, the advertised
87: issuer host is handled by core's `/` ingress and falls through to the SPA.
88: 
89: The dormant auth values cannot simply be re-enabled:
90: 
91: - issuer, resource, and CommonCal URL are all set to
92:   `https://cal.hajnal.space`, although the resource must be
93:   `https://mcal.hajnal.space/mcp`
94:   (`deploy/flux/overlays/production/charts/auth-helmrelease.yaml:34-47`);
95: - auth and core would both claim the same hostname and `/` prefix;
96: - the service requires PostgreSQL persistence and production secrets;
97: - its DCR callback policy currently admits a fixed lab loopback callback rather
98:   than the exact OpenCode loopback shape needed in production;
99: - lab-only test endpoints and callback helpers must not ship enabled.
100: 
101: ### 4. CommonCal consent and grant handling was proven only in the lab
102: 
103: The candidate authorization server redirects interactions to CommonCal
104: consent, but the production backend/frontend has no corresponding handoff and
105: consent flow. Helm contains dormant `authBridge` settings, but production code
106: does not implement their use.
107: 
108: Current grant-management endpoints are placeholders: list always returns an
109: empty array and create writes `user_id = 0`
110: (`backend/src/mcp_grant_management.rs:60-117`). The working, session-bound
111: consent/grant behavior exists only in `slice1-lab/src/bin/commoncal.rs`.
112: 
113: ### 5. Core's MCP internal API is not protected
114: 
115: The API-key validator is unused, and its current logic succeeds when the
116: expected secret is empty (`backend/src/mcp_internal.rs:206-223`). The entire
117: internal router is merged without authentication middleware
118: (`backend/src/main.rs:224-288`). Since the MCP server calls core through the
119: public HTTPS origin, this must be fixed before MCP is enabled in production.
120: 
121: ## Target architecture and decisions
122: 
123: 1. **Use `rmcp` in the production server.** Promote the proven SDK pattern;
124:    do not extend the hand-written JSON-RPC dispatcher.
125: 2. **Use a dedicated authorization-server hostname.** Default this plan to
126:    `https://auth.hajnal.space` to avoid the core SPA ingress. Confirm the final
127:    hostname before creating DNS/TLS and use that one value everywhere.
128: 3. **Use the standard token contract already proven by the lab.** Required:
129:    `iss`, numeric `sub`, exact MCP `aud`, `exp`, `iat`, `client_id`, and `scope`.
130:    Optional: `jti`, `amr`, and `acr`.
131: 4. **Keep CommonCal authoritative for users, sessions, calendar membership, and
132:    MCP grants.** The authorization server owns OAuth protocol state only.
133: 5. **Use PostgreSQL for authorization-server state.** This is the shortest path
134:    because the implemented adapter and resilience proofs already depend on it.
135: 6. **Pass identity per request/session.** Do not copy the lab's global
136:    `CURRENT_CLAIMS` slot (`slice1-lab/src/bin/mcp_echo.rs:46-62`); it is only
137:    safe for sequential lab traffic.
138: 
139: ## Implementation plan
140: 
141: ### Phase 0 — Add failing acceptance coverage
142: 
143: Dispatch this phase as four bounded tasks, in order, to keep the production
144: acceptance work independently runnable:
145: 
146: 1. `mcp-acceptance-harness-foundation` — target configuration, reusable
147:    fixtures, deterministic baseline `initialize` probe, and intentional current
148:    failure.
149: 2. `mcp-acceptance-discovery` — unauthenticated challenge plus public resource
150:    and authorization-server metadata assertions.
151: 3. `mcp-acceptance-oauth-lifecycle` — DCR, S256 PKCE, token exchange, and the
152:    authenticated MCP lifecycle through `calendar_list`.
153: 4. `mcp-acceptance-security-isolation` — negative token/grant cases and
154:    concurrent client identity isolation.
155: 
156: Phase 2 depends on task 4, so no protocol replacement is accepted without the
157: full Phase 0 regression harness in place.
158: 
159: Add black-box tests before changing behavior:
160: 
161: - unauthenticated `initialize` receives `401` with the public
162:   `resource_metadata` URL;
163: - protected-resource and authorization-server metadata are valid JSON;
164: - DCR, Authorization Code + S256 PKCE, and token exchange complete;
165: - authenticated `initialize`, `notifications/initialized`, `tools/list`, and
166:   `tools/call calendar_list` succeed;
167: - wrong issuer, audience, signature, expiry, client, missing grant, revoked
168:   grant, and broadened grant fail closed;
169: - two concurrent authenticated clients cannot observe each other's identity.
170: 
171: Build this as a production-component harness, reusing fixtures and assertions
172: from `slice1-lab`, rather than treating the lab binary itself as the release
173: artifact.
174: 
175: Exit gate: the new tests reproduce the current `initialize` failure and fail
176: for the expected reasons.
177: 
178: ### Phase 1 — Secure the core internal boundary
179: 
180: - Apply API-key middleware to the complete `/internal/mcp/*` router and any
181:   MCP-only reminder/token-exchange route.
182: - Fail startup when `MCP_INTERNAL_API_KEY` is absent or empty in production.
183: - Compare credentials in constant time and return `401` for missing/invalid
184:   keys without logging secret values.
185: - Confirm NetworkPolicy permits MCP-to-core traffic and denies unrelated pods;
186:   keep TLS on the current public service path unless a separately scoped
187:   private-service change is approved.
188: - Add route-level tests covering every protected route with missing, invalid,
189:   and valid keys.
190: 
191: Exit gate: no MCP internal operation is reachable without the configured key.
192: 
193: ### Phase 2 — Replace the custom MCP gateway with `rmcp`
194: 
195: - Mount `rmcp`'s Streamable HTTP service at `/mcp` and implement
196:   `ServerHandler`.
197: - Put bearer-token authentication around the complete MCP service so the first
198:   unauthenticated `initialize` receives the standards-compliant 401 challenge.
199: - Derive `resource_metadata` from `MCP_PUBLIC_RESOURCE_URL`; remove all
200:   loopback constants.
201: - Port all nine tools to typed SDK handlers with descriptions, complete JSON
202:   input schemas, MCP content blocks, request ids, and protocol error mapping.
203: - Preserve the existing domain behavior behind the handlers: live grant lookup,
204:   authorization, audit, rate limits, idempotency, and confirmation semantics.
205: - Store validated identity in request/session-safe context. Add a concurrency
206:   isolation test.
207: - Remove or retire the custom dispatcher after parity tests pass.
208: 
209: Also correct `calendar_list`'s permission mapping while porting it; it currently
210: checks the `availability_find` capability.
211: 
212: Exit gate: a generic Streamable HTTP client can complete the MCP lifecycle and
213: inspect valid schemas without authentication/context leakage.
214: 
215: ### Phase 3 — Align discovery and access-token validation
216: 
217: - Fetch `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` (and support the OIDC
218:   discovery form where appropriate), verify that returned `issuer` exactly
219:   matches configuration, then follow its HTTPS `jwks_uri`.
220: - Parse numeric `sub` as CommonCal user id and standard `client_id` and `scope`
221:   claims. Validate signature, allowed algorithm, `kid`, exact `iss`, exact MCP
222:   audience, `exp`, and `iat`; retain a small clock skew.
223: - Add bounded metadata/JWKS caching, key rotation overlap, and one refresh on an
224:   unknown `kid`. Never accept a stale key indefinitely.
225: - Keep grant lookup on every tool call so grant revocation takes effect even
226:   while an access token remains valid.
227: - Add integration tests that validate tokens issued by the repository's real
228:   authorization-server implementation, not hand-built lookalike fixtures only.
229: 
230: Exit gate: the candidate issuer's token is accepted, while every negative token
231: fixture is rejected with the correct public challenge.
232: 
233: ### Phase 4 — Promote consent and grant integration into core
234: 
235: - Port the lab's private interaction bridge client into the real backend using
236:   `AUTH_BRIDGE_URL`, timeout, and secret configuration.
237: - Add session-protected login continuation and consent endpoints/UI. Show the
238:   registered client, requested scopes, and calendars; never trust a user id from
239:   the browser payload.
240: - On approval, upsert exactly one active grant for the authenticated user and
241:   OAuth `client_id`, intersect requested scopes/calendars with the live allowed
242:   set, then resume the authorization interaction.
243: - On denial, create no grant. Make retries idempotent and prevent approval from
244:   broadening an existing grant accidentally.
245: - Replace all `user_id = 0` and empty-list placeholders. Make list, narrow, and
246:   revoke routes session-bound and ownership-checked.
247: - Preserve immediate revocation by checking the authoritative grant and live
248:   calendar membership for every tool invocation.
249: 
250: Exit gate: approve, deny, retry, narrow, cross-user, stale-membership, and revoke
251: tests from the lab pass against production core code.
252: 
253: ### Phase 5 — Productionize and deploy the authorization server
254: 
255: - Provision backed-up PostgreSQL and run the provider schema migration before
256:   enabling the deployment.
257: - Remove/disable lab test endpoints, loopback callback server, in-memory audit
258:   assumptions, and lab-named environment variables from the production entry
259:   point.
260: - Configure:
261:   - issuer: the chosen dedicated HTTPS hostname;
262:   - resource: `https://mcal.hajnal.space/mcp`;
263:   - CommonCal consent origin: `https://cal.hajnal.space`;
264:   - private bridge: cluster-only service with a rotated bearer secret;
265:   - short access-token lifetime, refresh rotation/reuse detection, revocation,
266:     signing-key overlap, request limits, and structured redaction.
267: - Configure DCR for OpenCode's actual callback behavior: loopback host, exact
268:   callback path, and permitted ephemeral port. Continue rejecting wildcards,
269:   arbitrary remote HTTPS redirects, and custom schemes unless explicitly
270:   approved.
271: - Add DNS and TLS for the dedicated issuer. Publish valid JSON authorization
272:   metadata and JWKS without any SPA fallback.
273: - Correct the dormant HelmRelease, NetworkPolicies, PDB, secrets, resource
274:   values, health checks, and Flux dependency order, then add it to the production
275:   kustomization only after its prerequisites exist.
276: 
277: Exit gate: discovery, DCR, PKCE, token issue, refresh, revocation, restart
278: persistence, and key overlap pass against the deployed issuer before MCP points
279: clients to it.
280: 
281: ### Phase 6 — Wire and validate the complete deployment
282: 
283: - Enable core's auth bridge and deploy the completed consent/grant code.
284: - Set the MCP protected-resource metadata and validator issuer to the dedicated
285:   authorization hostname. Add manifest tests asserting that issuer, audience,
286:   resource metadata, ingress host, and TLS host agree across charts.
287: - Deploy first to a production-equivalent environment and run the black-box
288:   harness through ingress, including concurrency and negative cases.
289: - Canary production, monitor auth error classes, initialization failures, grant
290:   denials, tool latency, provider storage health, and MCP/core 5xx rates.
291: 
292: Exit gate: the full acceptance matrix below passes through public production
293: URLs, not pod port-forwards.
294: 
295: ### Phase 7 — OpenCode acceptance and documentation
296: 
297: Validate with the supported OpenCode version and a clean OAuth cache:
298: 
299: ```sh
300: opencode mcp add commoncal-production --url https://mcal.hajnal.space/mcp
301: opencode mcp auth commoncal-production
302: opencode mcp list
303: ```
304: 
305: Complete browser login and consent, then verify:
306: 
307: 1. authenticated `initialize` negotiates a supported protocol version;
308: 2. `tools/list` returns all nine tools with schemas;
309: 3. `calendar_list` returns only calendars selected in the grant;
310: 4. narrowing or revoking the grant changes the next call immediately;
311: 5. restarting OpenCode refreshes/re-authorizes without manual token copying.
312: 
313: Update `docs/MCP-CONNECTION.md` only after this proof passes. It should explain
314: the OpenCode/LM Studio/Qwen roles and should not ask users for JWTs, internal API
315: keys, pod access, or a second MCP client.
316: 
317: ## Production acceptance matrix
318: 
319: | Area | Required result |
320: |---|---|
321: | MCP challenge | Unauthenticated `initialize` returns 401 and a public `resource_metadata` URL |
322: | Resource discovery | Protected-resource document is JSON and names the dedicated issuer |
323: | OAuth discovery | Authorization metadata is JSON with authorization, token, registration, and JWKS endpoints |
324: | Client registration | OpenCode DCR callback is accepted; unsafe redirect shapes are rejected |
325: | OAuth flow | Browser login + consent + S256 PKCE issues a resource-bound token |
326: | Token validation | Standard claims and exact issuer/audience validate; negative fixtures fail |
327: | MCP lifecycle | `initialize` and `notifications/initialized` succeed |
328: | Tool discovery | Nine tools have descriptions and complete input schemas |
329: | Authorization | Calls are limited by token scope, grant, live membership, and operation policy |
330: | Revocation | Grant revocation affects the next call; token/refresh revocation works |
331: | Isolation | Concurrent users/clients never share identity or session state |
332: | Internal API | Missing/invalid MCP API key is rejected on every protected core route |
333: | Persistence | OAuth state survives pod restart; migrations and backup/restore are proven |
334: | OpenCode | `mcp auth`, `mcp list`, and `calendar_list` succeed without token copying |
335: 
336: ## Rollout and rollback
337: 
338: Roll out in this order:
339: 
340: 1. core internal-API protection;
341: 2. PostgreSQL, issuer DNS/TLS, and authorization service without advertising it;
342: 3. production core consent/grant flow and private bridge;
343: 4. SDK-backed MCP deployment and production-equivalent end-to-end tests;
344: 5. protected-resource metadata/issuer cutover;
345: 6. OpenCode canary and general availability.
346: 
347: Keep prior core and MCP images, the previous issuer secret, and the Flux
348: revisions available during the canary. A rollback restores those revisions and
349: removes the new issuer from protected-resource metadata. OAuth key material and
350: the PostgreSQL volume must not be deleted during rollback. The existing MCP path
351: is already unavailable to standard clients, so rollback protects the calendar
352: application first; it does not constitute a working MCP fallback.
353: 
354: ## File map
355: 
356: Primary implementation areas:
357: 
358: - `mcp-server/src/main.rs` — mount SDK service and auth middleware
359: - `mcp-server/src/gateway.rs` — retire custom protocol dispatcher; retain reusable policy logic
360: - `mcp-server/src/oauth.rs` — discovery, standard claims, JWKS cache/rotation
361: - `mcp-server/src/tools/` — typed SDK tools and schemas
362: - `backend/src/mcp_internal.rs` and `backend/src/main.rs` — fail-closed internal API boundary
363: - `backend/src/mcp_grant_management.rs` — real session-owned grant management
364: - backend/frontend HTTP routes — login continuation and consent UI
365: - `slice1-lab/auth-server/` — promote into a production authorization-service package
366: - `deploy/helm/commoncal-auth/` — production auth chart
367: - `deploy/helm/commoncal/` — auth bridge and core secret/network wiring
368: - `deploy/helm/commoncal-mcp/` — public resource/issuer wiring
369: - `deploy/flux/overlays/production/` — issuer ingress, dependencies, and rollout
370: - `slice1-lab/` — reusable proof fixtures; not a production binary
371: 
372: ## Prerequisites and explicit decision gates
373: 
374: Work may begin on tests, internal API security, MCP SDK adoption, and core
375: consent code immediately. Production cutover is blocked until all of these are
376: decided or supplied:
377: 
378: - final dedicated issuer hostname and DNS/TLS ownership;
379: - PostgreSQL hosting, backups, and restore procedure;
380: - production OAuth signing keys, cookie keys, and bridge-key rotation process;
381: - the supported OpenCode version and its observed loopback callback shape;
382: - consent UI/product copy and the initial scope defaults.
383: 
384: ## Definition of done
385: 
386: The fix is complete only when a clean OpenCode installation can add the remote
387: server, authenticate through the browser, approve a constrained grant, list the
388: nine MCP tools, and call `calendar_list` against production—without copying a
389: token, using `MCP_INTERNAL_API_KEY`, port-forwarding a pod, or installing a
390: second MCP client—and all negative/security tests remain green.

# Production MCP connection fix plan

Status: proposed  
Prepared: 2026-09-17  
Target client: OpenCode (using LM Studio/Qwen as its model provider)

call CommonCal tools.

OpenCode is already the MCP client. LM Studio supplies the model and Qwen is the
model; neither replaces the MCP client. No additional MCP client is required.
MCP Inspector may be used only as an independent diagnostic tool.

## Verified current state

Production was probed on 2026-09-17:

- `POST /mcp` with `initialize` reaches the service but returns JSON-RPC
  `-32601 Method not found`.
- unauthenticated `tools/list` returns nine names, without complete MCP tool
  schemas.
- unauthenticated `tools/call` returns `401`, but its `WWW-Authenticate` header
  points to `http://127.0.0.1:3001/...` rather than the public production URL.
- protected-resource metadata at
  `https://mcal.hajnal.space/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` is valid JSON
  and advertises `https://cal.hajnal.space` as the authorization server.
- `https://cal.hajnal.space/.well-known/openid-configuration` returns the
  CommonCal SPA HTML, not authorization-server metadata.
- `opencode mcp auth commoncal-production` fails on `initialize` before OAuth
  discovery can begin.

This means production is reachable but is not currently connectable by a
standard MCP client.

## Confirmed root causes

### 1. Production does not implement the MCP lifecycle

The production route mounts a custom Axum handler
(`mcp-server/src/main.rs:54-78`). Its dispatcher recognizes only `tools/list`
and `tools/call`; every other method, including `initialize`, returns `-32601`
(`mcp-server/src/gateway.rs:103-185`). Authentication is performed only inside
the `tools/call` branch (`mcp-server/src/gateway.rs:214-254`), so OpenCode never
receives an OAuth challenge for its initial request.

The custom wire responses are also incomplete:

- `tools/list` emits only `{ "name": ... }`, with no description or
  `inputSchema`, and does not preserve the JSON-RPC request id
  (`mcp-server/src/gateway.rs:187-212`).
- tool results use project-specific serialization rather than SDK-generated MCP
  content/result envelopes.

`rmcp` is already a production dependency, and the repository contains a
working SDK-backed reference in `slice1-lab/src/bin/mcp_echo.rs`. That lab
supports initialization, Streamable HTTP sessions, typed schemas, OAuth
middleware, and all tool categories. It explicitly says it is not the
production server (`slice1-lab/src/bin/mcp_echo.rs:1-13`).

### 2. The production OAuth challenge and JWT contract are inconsistent

Both production 401 builders hard-code the lab protected-resource URL
(`mcp-server/src/gateway.rs:456-541`).

The JWT validator says it uses discovery, but actually fetches
`<issuer>/.well-known/oauth-jwks` directly
(`mcp-server/src/oauth.rs:304-350`). It must instead fetch authorization-server
metadata and follow its `jwks_uri`.

Production also requires private namespaced claims such as
`https://commoncal.tld/user_id` and a custom scope array
(`mcp-server/src/oauth.rs:24-46,158-177`). The proven authorization server and
lab validator use standard claims: numeric `sub`, `client_id`, space-delimited
`scope`, `jti`, and `amr` (`slice1-lab/src/jwt.rs:12-33,147-184`). A token from
the repository's own authorization server would therefore still be rejected by
the production MCP server.

### 3. The authorization service is not deployed or routed in production

The production Flux kustomization includes only core and MCP
(`deploy/flux/overlays/production/kustomization.yaml:3-5`). The existing auth
HelmRelease is excluded and was deliberately removed because PostgreSQL was not
available (`deploy/PROBLEM-02-remove-auth.md`). Consequently, the advertised
issuer host is handled by core's `/` ingress and falls through to the SPA.

The dormant auth values cannot simply be re-enabled:

- issuer, resource, and CommonCal URL are all set to
  `https://cal.hajnal.space`, although the resource must be
  `https://mcal.hajnal.space/mcp`
  (`deploy/flux/overlays/production/charts/auth-helmrelease.yaml:34-47`);
- auth and core would both claim the same hostname and `/` prefix;
- the service requires PostgreSQL persistence and production secrets;
- its DCR callback policy currently admits a fixed lab loopback callback rather
  than the exact OpenCode loopback shape needed in production;
- lab-only test endpoints and callback helpers must not ship enabled.

### 4. CommonCal consent and grant handling was proven only in the lab

The candidate authorization server redirects interactions to CommonCal
consent, but the production backend/frontend has no corresponding handoff and
consent flow. Helm contains dormant `authBridge` settings, but production code
does not implement their use.

Current grant-management endpoints are placeholders: list always returns an
empty array and create writes `user_id = 0`
(`backend/src/mcp_grant_management.rs:60-117`). The working, session-bound
consent/grant behavior exists only in `slice1-lab/src/bin/commoncal.rs`.

### 5. Core's MCP internal API is not protected

The API-key validator is unused, and its current logic succeeds when the
expected secret is empty (`backend/src/mcp_internal.rs:206-223`). The entire
internal router is merged without authentication middleware
(`backend/src/main.rs:224-288`). Since the MCP server calls core through the
public HTTPS origin, this must be fixed before MCP is enabled in production.

## Target architecture and decisions

1. **Use `rmcp` in the production server.** Promote the proven SDK pattern;
   do not extend the hand-written JSON-RPC dispatcher.
2. **Use a dedicated authorization-server hostname.** Default this plan to
   `https://auth.hajnal.space` to avoid the core SPA ingress. Confirm the final
   hostname before creating DNS/TLS and use that one value everywhere.
3. **Use the standard token contract already proven by the lab.** Required:

acceptance work independently runnable:

1. `mcp-acceptance-harness-foundation` — target configuration, reusable

   failure.
2. `mcp-acceptance-discovery` — unauthenticated challenge plus public resource
   and authorization-server metadata assertions.
3. `mcp-acceptance-oauth-lifecycle` — DCR, S256 PKCE, token exchange, and the
   authenticated MCP lifecycle through `calendar_list`.
4. `mcp-acceptance-security-isolation` — negative token/grant cases and
   concurrent client identity isolation.

Phase 2 depends on task 4, so no protocol replacement is accepted without the
full Phase 0 regression harness in place.

- unauthenticated `initialize` receives `401` with the public
  `resource_metadata` URL;
- protected-resource and authorization-server metadata are valid JSON;
- DCR, Authorization Code + S256 PKCE, and token exchange complete;
- authenticated `initialize`, `notifications/initialized`, `tools/list`, and

- wrong issuer, audience, signature, expiry, client, missing grant, revoked
  grant, and broadened grant fail closed;
- two concurrent authenticated clients cannot observe each other's identity.

from `slice1-lab`, rather than treating the lab binary itself as the release
artifact.

for the expected reasons.

- Apply API-key middleware to the complete `/internal/mcp/*` router and any
  MCP-only reminder/token-exchange route.
- Fail startup when `MCP_INTERNAL_API_KEY` is absent or empty in production.
- Compare credentials in constant time and return `401` for missing/invalid
  keys without logging secret values.
- Confirm NetworkPolicy permits MCP-to-core traffic and denies unrelated pods;
  keep TLS on the current public service path unless a separately scoped
  private-service change is approved.
- Add route-level tests covering every protected route with missing, invalid,
  and valid keys.

Exit gate: no MCP internal operation is reachable without the configured key.

  `ServerHandler`.
- Put bearer-token authentication around the complete MCP service so the first
  unauthenticated `initialize` receives the standards-compliant 401 challenge.
- Derive `resource_metadata` from `MCP_PUBLIC_RESOURCE_URL`; remove all
  loopback constants.
- Port all nine tools to typed SDK handlers with descriptions, complete JSON
  input schemas, MCP content blocks, request ids, and protocol error mapping.
- Preserve the existing domain behavior behind the handlers: live grant lookup,
  authorization, audit, rate limits, idempotency, and confirmation semantics.
- Store validated identity in request/session-safe context. Add a concurrency
  isolation test.

inspect valid schemas without authentication/context leakage.

  matches configuration, then follow its HTTPS `jwks_uri`.

  claims. Validate signature, allowed algorithm, `kid`, exact `iss`, exact MCP
  audience, `exp`, and `iat`; retain a small clock skew.

  unknown `kid`. Never accept a stale key indefinitely.
- Keep grant lookup on every tool call so grant revocation takes effect even
  while an access token remains valid.
- Add integration tests that validate tokens issued by the repository's real
  authorization-server implementation, not hand-built lookalike fixtures only.

fixture is rejected with the correct public challenge.

### Phase 4 — Promote consent and grant integration into core

- Port the lab's private interaction bridge client into the real backend using
  `AUTH_BRIDGE_URL`, timeout, and secret configuration.
- Add session-protected login continuation and consent endpoints/UI. Show the
  registered client, requested scopes, and calendars; never trust a user id from
  the browser payload.
- On approval, upsert exactly one active grant for the authenticated user and
  OAuth `client_id`, intersect requested scopes/calendars with the live allowed
  set, then resume the authorization interaction.
- On denial, create no grant. Make retries idempotent and prevent approval from
  broadening an existing grant accidentally.
- Replace all `user_id = 0` and empty-list placeholders. Make list, narrow, and
  revoke routes session-bound and ownership-checked.
- Preserve immediate revocation by checking the authoritative grant and live
  calendar membership for every tool invocation.

tests from the lab pass against production core code.

  enabling the deployment.

  assumptions, and lab-named environment variables from the production entry
  point.

  arbitrary remote HTTPS redirects, and custom schemes unless explicitly
  approved.

  metadata and JWKS without any SPA fallback.

  values, health checks, and Flux dependency order, then add it to the production

  authorization hostname. Add manifest tests asserting that issuer, audience,
  resource metadata, ingress host, and TLS host agree across charts.

- Canary production, monitor auth error classes, initialization failures, grant

opencode mcp auth commoncal-production
opencode mcp list

1. authenticated `initialize` negotiates a supported protocol version;
2. `tools/list` returns all nine tools with schemas;
3. `calendar_list` returns only calendars selected in the grant;
4. narrowing or revoking the grant changes the next call immediately;
5. restarting OpenCode refreshes/re-authorizes without manual token copying.

Update `docs/MCP-CONNECTION.md` only after this proof passes. It should explain
the OpenCode/LM Studio/Qwen roles and should not ask users for JWTs, internal API
keys, pod access, or a second MCP client.

## Production acceptance matrix

| Area | Required result |
|---|---|
| MCP challenge | Unauthenticated `initialize` returns 401 and a public `resource_metadata` URL |
| Resource discovery | Protected-resource document is JSON and names the dedicated issuer |
| OAuth discovery | Authorization metadata is JSON with authorization, token, registration, and JWKS endpoints |
| Client registration | OpenCode DCR callback is accepted; unsafe redirect shapes are rejected |
| OAuth flow | Browser login + consent + S256 PKCE issues a resource-bound token |
| Token validation | Standard claims and exact issuer/audience validate; negative fixtures fail |
| MCP lifecycle | `initialize` and `notifications/initialized` succeed |
| Tool discovery | Nine tools have descriptions and complete input schemas |
| Authorization | Calls are limited by token scope, grant, live membership, and operation policy |
| Revocation | Grant revocation affects the next call; token/refresh revocation works |
| Isolation | Concurrent users/clients never share identity or session state |
| Internal API | Missing/invalid MCP API key is rejected on every protected core route |
| Persistence | OAuth state survives pod restart; migrations and backup/restore are proven |
| OpenCode | `mcp auth`, `mcp list`, and `calendar_list` succeed without token copying |

## Rollout and rollback

Roll out in this order:

1. core internal-API protection;
2. PostgreSQL, issuer DNS/TLS, and authorization service without advertising it;
3. production core consent/grant flow and private bridge;
4. SDK-backed MCP deployment and production-equivalent end-to-end tests;
5. protected-resource metadata/issuer cutover;
6. OpenCode canary and general availability.

Keep prior core and MCP images, the previous issuer secret, and the Flux
revisions available during the canary. A rollback restores those revisions and
removes the new issuer from protected-resource metadata. OAuth key material and
the PostgreSQL volume must not be deleted during rollback. The existing MCP path
is already unavailable to standard clients, so rollback protects the calendar
application first; it does not constitute a working MCP fallback.

## File map

Primary implementation areas:

- `mcp-server/src/main.rs` — mount SDK service and auth middleware
- `mcp-server/src/gateway.rs` — retire custom protocol dispatcher; retain reusable policy logic
- `mcp-server/src/oauth.rs` — discovery, standard claims, JWKS cache/rotation
- `mcp-server/src/tools/` — typed SDK tools and schemas
- `backend/src/mcp_internal.rs` and `backend/src/main.rs` — fail-closed internal API boundary
- `backend/src/mcp_grant_management.rs` — real session-owned grant management
- backend/frontend HTTP routes — login continuation and consent UI
- `slice1-lab/auth-server/` — promote into a production authorization-service package
- `deploy/helm/commoncal-auth/` — production auth chart
- `deploy/helm/commoncal/` — auth bridge and core secret/network wiring
- `deploy/helm/commoncal-mcp/` — public resource/issuer wiring
- `deploy/flux/overlays/production/` — issuer ingress, dependencies, and rollout
- `slice1-lab/` — reusable proof fixtures; not a production binary

## Prerequisites and explicit decision gates

Work may begin on tests, internal API security, MCP SDK adoption, and core
consent code immediately. Production cutover is blocked until all of these are
decided or supplied:

- final dedicated issuer hostname and DNS/TLS ownership;
- PostgreSQL hosting, backups, and restore procedure;
- production OAuth signing keys, cookie keys, and bridge-key rotation process;
- the supported OpenCode version and its observed loopback callback shape;
- consent UI/product copy and the initial scope defaults.

## Definition of done

The fix is complete only when a clean OpenCode installation can add the remote
server, authenticate through the browser, approve a constrained grant, list the
nine MCP tools, and call `calendar_list` against production—without copying a
token, using `MCP_INTERNAL_API_KEY`, port-forwarding a pod, or installing a
second MCP client—and all negative/security tests remain green.

222: /// Constant-time byte comparison to avoid timing side channels.
223: fn constant_time_eq(a: &[u8], b: &[u8]) -> bool {
224:     if a.len() != b.len() {
225:         return false;
226:     }
227:     let mut diff = 0u8;
228:     for (x, y) in a.iter().zip(b.iter()) {
229:         diff |= x ^ y;
230:     }
231:     diff == 0
232: }

234: fn unauthorized_response() -> Response {
235:     Response::builder()
236:         .status(StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED)
237:         .header("content-type", "application/json")
238:         .body(axum::body::Body::from(
239:             serde_json::json!({ "error": "unauthorized" }).to_string(),
240:         ))
241:         .expect("static response cannot fail to build")
242: }

244: /// Middleware enforcing the `x-mcp-api-key` header on MCP internal routes.
245: ///
246: /// Fails closed: when no key is configured, every request is rejected.
247: /// Returns 401 for missing or invalid keys and never logs key material.
248: pub async fn mcp_api_key_middleware(
249:     State(auth): State<McpApiKeyAuth>,
250:     request: Request,
251:     next: Next,
252: ) -> Response {
253:     if auth.expected_key.is_empty() {
254:         return unauthorized_response();
255:     }
256:     let provided = request
257:         .headers()
258:         .get("x-mcp-api-key")
259:         .and_then(|value| value.to_str().ok())
260:         .unwrap_or("");
261:     if constant_time_eq(provided.as_bytes(), auth.expected_key.as_bytes()) {
262:         return next.run(request).await;
263:     }
264:     unauthorized_response()
265: }

338: /// RFC 8693 token exchange endpoint.
339: pub async fn token_exchange(
340:     State(pool): State<SqlitePool>,
341:     Query(params): Query<TokenExchangeQuery>,
342:     headers: axum::http::HeaderMap,
343: ) -> Result<Json<TokenExchangeResponse>, (StatusCode, String)> {
344:     let _ = pool;
345:     let _ = headers;
346: 
347:     if params.grant_type != "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange" {
348:         return Err((
349:             StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST,
350:             "unsupported grant type".to_string(),
351:         ));
352:     }
353: 
354:     if params.subject_token.is_empty() {
355:         return Err((StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST, "missing subject_token".to_string()));
356:     }
357: 
358:     // Generate a short-lived internal access token.
359:     let internal_token = uuid::Uuid::new_v4().to_string();
360: 
361:     Ok(Json(TokenExchangeResponse {
362:         access_token: internal_token,
363:         token_type: "mcp_internal".to_string(),
364:         expires_in: 300,
365:         scope: params.scope.unwrap_or_default(),
366:     }))

567:     /// Compute availability slots for a calendar in [from, to].
568:     /// A slot is "busy" if an event overlaps it, otherwise "free".
569:     /// Slots are 1-hour blocks aligned to the hour.
570:     async fn compute_availability(
571:         &self,
572:         calendar_id: i64,
573:         from: &str,
574:         to: &str,
575:     ) -> Vec<serde_json::Value> {
576:         let from_ts = Self::parse_ts(from).unwrap_or(0);
577:         let to_ts = Self::parse_ts(to).unwrap_or(0);
578:         let events: Vec<Event> = {
579:             let st = self.inner.read().await;
580:             st.events
581:                 .values()
582:                 .filter(|e| e.calendar_id == calendar_id)
583:                 .cloned()
584:                 .collect()
585:         };
586: 
587:         let mut slots = Vec::new();
588:         let mut t = from_ts;
589:         while t < to_ts {
590:             let slot_end = (t + 3600).min(to_ts);
591:             let busy = events.iter().any(|e| {
592:                 e.start_utc.is_some_and(|s| s < slot_end) && e.end_utc.is_some_and(|en| en > t)
593:             });
594:             slots.push(serde_json::json!({
595:                 "start": t,
596:                 "end": slot_end,
597:                 "status": if busy { "busy" } else { "free" },
598:             }));
599:             t = slot_end;
600:         }
601:         slots
602:     }

882:     /// Decide a handoff (login/consent/deny) via the auth server's private API.
883:     /// `subject` is the authenticated CommonCal user id (the identity authority
884:     /// is CommonCal; the auth server binds the provider grant to this subject
885:     /// rather than a hardcoded value). Returns the resume URL.
886:     ///
887:     /// Honors the lab bridge-failure test hook: if armed, this call fails
888:     /// (simulating a bridge timeout) and the hook decrements, so a retry
889:     /// succeeds — proving grant-first / bridge-second idempotent retry.
890:     async fn decide_interaction(
891:         &self,
892:         handoff: &str,
893:         kind: &str,
894:         subject: Option<i64>,
895:     ) -> Result<String, String> {
896:         // Lab test hook: simulate a bridge failure on the next CONSENT decide
897:         // call(s). Only consent decisions are affected — the grant-first /
898:         // bridge-second ordering is a consent-path property, and login decisions
899:         // must not be disrupted (they precede the grant write).
900:         if kind == "consent" {
901:             let mut st = self.inner.write().await;
902:             if st.decide_fail_remaining > 0 {
903:                 st.decide_fail_remaining -= 1;
904:                 tracing::warn!("simulating bridge decide failure (test hook)");
905:                 return Err("simulated bridge timeout (test hook)".to_string());
906:             }
907:         }
908: 
909:         let url = format!(
910:             "{}/internal/interactions/{}",
911:             self.auth_private_base,
912:             urlencoding::encode(handoff)
913:         );
914:         let mut body = serde_json::json!({ "kind": kind });
915:         if let Some(sub) = subject {
916:             body["subject"] = serde_json::json!(sub);
917:         }
918:         let resp = self
919:             .http
920:             .put(&url)
921:             .header("Authorization", format!("Bearer {}", self.bridge_key))
922:             .json(&body)
923:             .send()
924:             .await
925:             .map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
926:         let status = resp.status();
927:         if !status.is_success() {
928:             let text = resp.text().await.unwrap_or_default();
929:             tracing::error!(status = %status, text = %text, "decide_interaction failed");
930:             return Err(format!("interaction decide failed: {status} {text}"));
931:         }
932:         let result: serde_json::Value = resp.json().await.map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
933:         result
934:             .get("resumeUrl")
935:             .and_then(|v| v.as_str())
936:             .map(|s| s.to_string())
937:             .ok_or_else(|| "decide response missing resumeUrl".to_string())
938:     }
939: }
